figures.caption: FIG. 1. (a) m(k) (solid lines) and h(k) (broken lines) for RONs with N = 1600, α = 0.9. The dotted lines are the mean-field curves of Eq. (25). (b) ∆(k) for RONs with α = 0.9. For each condition, m(k) and h(k) are averaged over 100 realizations of RONs.

FIG. 5. MCϵ and HMCϵ for the three linear reservoirs with N = 800, α = 0.9, and ϵ = 0.1. (a) DSRN. A single realization of a DSRN is used to compute MCϵ(= HMCϵ) numerically. The solid line is Eq. (32). (b) RON. The solid line is Eq. (33). (c) RGN. In panels (b) and (c), MCϵ and HMCϵ are averaged over 100 realizations of each linear reservoir.

FIG. 7. mϵ(k) and hϵ(k) for a single realization of an RGN. (a) β = 5.0× 10−4. (b) β = 5.0× 10−3. The other parameters are the same as in Fig. 5(c).

FIG. 8. Dependence of the eigenvalues of C on β for (a) a RON (b) an RGN. 20 eigenvalues µ1+10i (i = 0, 1, . . . , 19) are shown. The eigenvalues are obtained from a single realization of a RON and an RGN in Figs. 5(b) and 5(c), respectively.

FIG. 10. m(k) (solid lines) and h(k) (broken lines) estimated by numerical simulations of Eq. (1) over finite time lengths T = 10000, 20000 for (a) RONs and (b) RGNs with N = 800, α = 0.9, and β = 0.01. Both quantities are averaged over 20 trials with random initial conditions. In each trial, the initial 1000 time steps are ignored. The values of m(k) and h(k) calculated from the theoretical formulas of pk and C [Eqs. (19) and (20), respectively] are also shown. Horizontal lines are the theoretical predictions of the overestimates of m(k) (solid lines) and h(k) (broken lines) when they are close to zero (The upper and lower lines are for T = 10000 and T = 20000, respectively).
